description.en: The 45-degree back extension performs back extensions on a dedicated 45-degree hyperextension bench. You lower your torso forward by hinging at the hips, then extend back up. The 45-degree angle provides a different resistance profile than flat or horizontal back extensions.

en: Set up on a 45-degree back extension bench. Hips on the pad, feet locked.
Cross arms over your chest or place hands behind your head.
Lower your torso forward by hinging at the hips.
Continue until your torso is roughly perpendicular to your legs.
Extend back up by contracting your erector spinae and glutes.
Rise until your body is in line with the bench angle.
Do not hyperextend past the bench angle.
Aim for 12 to 15 reps. Hold a plate for added resistance.
Builds erector spinae and glute strength
Consistent 45-degree resistance profile
Easy to add weight with a plate
Available in most gyms
Develops lower back endurance
Useful for back health

description.en: The ab mat sit-up is a sit-up variation performed with a small curved foam pad (ab mat) under the lower back. The pad supports the natural arch of the lumbar spine and allows the torso to extend slightly below horizontal at the bottom, creating a longer range of motion and stronger ab contraction than a flat-floor sit-up. It is a staple exercise in CrossFit.

en: Place an ab mat (or a folded towel) on the floor. Sit on the floor with the mat positioned just below your lower back.
Lie back so the mat supports your lumbar spine. Your shoulders should rest just behind the mat on the floor.
Bend your knees and bring the soles of your feet together in a butterfly position. This stabilizes you without engaging the hip flexors heavily.
Place your hands behind your head with fingers lightly touching, or extend them overhead.
Brace your core and tuck your chin slightly.
Sit up by curling your torso forward. Drive through your abs to bring your hands to or past your feet.
At the top, your torso should be roughly upright. Squeeze your abs hard.
Lower your torso under control back to the start position. Touch your shoulders to the floor behind the mat before the next rep.
Longer range of motion than flat-floor sit-ups
Supports the lumbar spine and reduces lower-back strain
Butterfly leg position reduces hip flexor dominance
Builds the rectus abdominis through full range
Easy to scale by adding weight (chest hold or overhead)
Standard CrossFit movement with established progression standards

musclesWorked: Hip flexors (less than standard sit-up due to butterfly position)

description.en: Agility ball drills use a reaction ball — a small rubber ball with bumps that bounces unpredictably — to train reaction speed, hand-eye coordination, and athletic awareness. The unpredictable bounce forces quick adjustments and builds the cognitive speed essential for sports performance.

en: Stand 5 to 10 feet from a wall with a reaction ball in your hand.
Throw the ball at the wall with moderate force.
The ball will bounce off the wall and the floor in unpredictable directions due to its bumpy shape.
Track the ball with your eyes and react to catch it before it hits the ground twice.
Stay in an athletic stance — knees bent, ready to move quickly.
Continue throwing and catching for 30 to 60 seconds per set.
Vary throwing force, angle, and distance for different reactions.
For partner drills, have a partner toss the ball at unpredictable angles.
Trains reaction speed and hand-eye coordination
Builds cognitive speed for sports
Develops quick directional changes
Improves focus and concentration
Fun and engaging training
Useful for athletes in reactive sports

description.en: The barbell press sit-up combines a weighted sit-up with an overhead barbell press at the top position. You hold a barbell at your chest, sit up, then press the bar overhead before lowering back down. It builds ab strength and overhead pressing power in one compound movement.

en: Lie on the floor with knees bent, feet anchored. Hold a barbell at your chest.
Sit up by flexing your spine. Bring your chest toward your knees.
At the top of the sit-up, press the barbell overhead to lockout.
Lower the bar back to your chest.
Lower your torso back to the floor under control.
That is one rep.
Use light to moderate weight. Aim for 8 to 12 reps.
Keep feet anchored throughout.
Combines sit-up with overhead press
Builds abs and shoulders together
Compound movement — time-efficient
Different stimulus than either exercise alone
Easy to scale by weight
Engaging core-to-press combo

description.en: The barbell weighted front chest squat is performed with the barbell held vertically against the chest, hugged with both arms wrapped around it. The position forces an extremely upright torso while allowing heavy loading. It builds quad strength and core engagement and is useful for lifters with limited wrist mobility.

en: Stand a barbell on end and hug it to your chest with both arms wrapped around it.
Hold the bar vertically against your chest with elbows tucked tight.
Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart.
Brace your core hard and lift your chest.
Squat down by sitting back and bending your knees.
Maintain an upright torso to keep the bar pressed to your chest.
Descend until your thighs are parallel to the floor or deeper.
Drive up through your heels to return to standing.
Forces upright torso for safer squat mechanics
Builds strong core engagement
Emphasizes quad development
Alternative for lifters with wrist mobility issues
Strong arm and grip workout from holding the bar
Allows heavier loading than goblet squats

description.en: The barbell wide squat uses a stance significantly wider than shoulder-width with toes turned out. The wider stance shifts emphasis to the adductors and glutes while requiring less ankle mobility than narrow squats. It is popular in powerlifting.

en: Set a barbell at upper-back height. Step under and position it across your upper traps.
Unrack the bar. Set your feet 1.5 to 2 times shoulder-width, toes turned out 30 to 45 degrees.
Brace your core. Lift your chest.
Sit your hips back and down. Push your knees out toward your toes.
Descend to parallel or below.
Drive through your full foot to stand. Squeeze your glutes at the top.
Keep your torso as upright as possible.
Wider stance allows heavier loading for many lifters.
Shifts emphasis to adductors and glutes
Requires less ankle mobility than narrow squats
Popular in powerlifting
Often allows heavier loading
Builds hip strength in the frontal plane
Different stimulus for squat programming

description.en: The bodyweight standing military press creates resistance by pressing one fist into the opposite palm and pushing both hands overhead together. The constant tension between the hands gives the shoulders a hard isometric and dynamic workout. It is a useful no-equipment shoulder builder.

en: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart.
Make a fist with one hand and place it inside the open palm of the other hand at chest level.
Press the fist into the palm to create constant tension.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Press both hands together straight overhead.
Maintain the isometric pressure between the hands throughout.
Lock out at the top with arms straight.
Lower the hands slowly back to chest level.
No equipment required
Builds shoulder strength
Self-resistance training
Useful for travel or home
Builds isometric shoulder power
Joint-friendly variation

description.en: The bottle weighted swing is a hip hinge swing performed with a weighted bottle or water jug instead of a kettlebell. The bottle swings between the legs and is powered up to chest height with the hips. It is a great at-home posterior chain builder.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a weighted jug with both hands.
Let the jug hang between your legs with arms straight.
Hinge at the hips to swing the jug back between your legs.
Drive your hips forward explosively to power the jug forward.
Let the jug rise to chest height as the hips lock out.
Keep your arms relaxed and let the hips do the work.
Allow the jug to swing back down between the legs.
Continue the rhythm with smooth hip drive.
Builds posterior chain
No KB needed
Trains hip hinge
Strong at-home option
Easy to scale loading
Travel-friendly setup

description.en: The box jump down with single-leg stabilization is a plyometric exercise where you jump off a box and land on a single leg, holding the landing for control. It trains eccentric loading, deceleration, and single-leg stability — critical skills for injury prevention in athletes.

en: Stand on top of a sturdy box (12 to 24 inches high). Feet shoulder-width apart.
Step or hop forward off the box.
As you descend, prepare to land on one leg only.
Land softly on your right leg with a bent knee to absorb the impact.
“Stick” the landing — hold balance for 2 to 3 seconds without wobbling.
Step back onto the box. Repeat with the same leg or alternate.
Focus on quiet, soft landings. The hold is the key element.
Use a low box to start (12 inches) and progress higher as control improves.
Trains deceleration and landing mechanics
Builds single-leg stability under impact
Critical for injury prevention in jumping athletes
Develops eccentric strength
Builds confidence in single-leg landings
Excellent rehab and prehab exercise

description.en: The bridge hip abduction performs a glute bridge while actively pushing the knees outward (hip abduction). A band around the knees provides resistance. It activates both the gluteus maximus (bridge) and gluteus medius (abduction) simultaneously.

en: Place a mini band around both thighs above the knees.
Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat.
Bridge your hips up while pushing your knees outward against the band.
Squeeze both glute max and glute medius at the top.
Lower under control while maintaining outward knee pressure.
The band adds abduction resistance throughout.
Aim for 12 to 20 reps.
Excellent glute activation exercise.
Activates glute max and medius simultaneously
Band adds abduction challenge
Excellent warm-up before leg training
Builds complete glute activation
Develops hip stability
Easy to set up

description.en: The cable kneeling preacher curl combines the preacher pad with a low cable station. Kneeling behind the preacher bench with your arms over the pad, you curl a cable attachment for strict bicep work with the constant tension of cables. The combination is one of the strictest bicep variations.

en: Set a preacher bench in front of a low cable pulley.
Attach a straight bar or rope to the low pulley.
Kneel behind the preacher bench with your chest pressed to the pad.
Drape your arms over the preacher pad with the cable attachment in your hands.
Allow your arms to fully extend with the cable below.
Brace your core and pin your chest to the pad.
Curl the attachment up by bending only at the elbows.
Squeeze the biceps at the top, then lower with control to full extension.
Strict bicep isolation
Constant cable tension
Strong stretch at the bottom
Eliminates body english
Builds bicep size with peak contraction
Useful for hypertrophy training

description.en: The cable reverse curl is a forearm and brachialis exercise performed at a low cable pulley with a straight bar using an overhand (pronated) grip. The overhand grip shifts emphasis from the biceps brachii to the brachialis and forearm extensors. The cable provides constant tension throughout.

en: Attach a straight bar to a low cable pulley. Stand facing the machine with feet hip-width apart.
Grip the bar with an overhand (palms-down) grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Stand tall. Pin your elbows against your sides. Brace your core.
Curl the bar up by bending at the elbows. Keep the overhand grip throughout.
Continue until the bar reaches shoulder height. Squeeze hard at the top.
Lower under control. Maintain cable tension.
Use lighter weight than standard curls — the overhand position is harder.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Targets the brachialis and forearm extensors with constant tension
Builds arm thickness and forearm size
Balances out bicep-dominant training
Helps prevent tennis elbow by strengthening forearm extensors
Easy to load progressively
Complements standard curls for complete arm development

description.en: The cable shoulder 90 degrees internal rotation is a rotator cuff drill done with the upper arm at ninety degrees of abduction. The lifter rotates the forearm downward against cable tension. It builds the internal rotators and shoulder stability.

en: Set a cable to head height with a single handle attached.
Stand sideways to the cable with the working arm closest.
Lift the working arm out to the side at shoulder height.
Bend the elbow at ninety degrees with the forearm pointing up.
Brace your core and keep the upper arm parallel to the floor.
Rotate the forearm down toward the floor.
Hold briefly at the rotated position.
Return with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Trains internal rotation
Builds the rotator cuff
Strong shoulder drill
Useful for shoulder care
Builds shoulder stability

description.en: The cable shoulder internal rotation isolates the subscapularis (one of the four rotator cuff muscles) using a low cable. You stand sideways to the cable with your elbow pinned to your side and rotate your forearm across your body. It is critical for rotator cuff balance — most people overtrain external rotation while neglecting internal.

en: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position. Attach a D-handle.
Stand sideways to the pulley with the cable on your right side. Grip the handle with your right hand.
Pin your right elbow firmly against your right side. Bend your right elbow at 90 degrees with your forearm parallel to the floor.
Step away from the pulley until the cable is under tension and your right forearm is rotated outward (palm facing right).
Brace your core.
Rotate your right forearm across your body, keeping your elbow pinned to your side.
Continue until your right hand reaches your stomach (palm now facing your body).
Slowly return to the start over two seconds. Use very light weight — the rotator cuff is small.
Isolates the internal rotators of the rotator cuff
Balances out external rotation work
Improves shoulder stability
Useful prehab and rehab exercise
Constant cable tension
Easy to scale with light loads

description.en: The Cossack squat is a deep lateral squat where you shift all your weight to one leg in a wide stance, lowering into a deep squat on the working leg while the opposite leg stays extended straight. It builds hip mobility, adductor flexibility, and unilateral leg strength. It is a staple in athletic mobility routines.

en: Stand with feet much wider than shoulder-width, toes pointing forward or slightly out.
Shift your weight to the right by bending your right knee while keeping your left leg straight.
Lower into a deep squat on your right leg. Your left leg extends straight to the side with the foot flexed (toes up).
Keep your right heel flat on the floor. Sit your right hip back and down.
Hold the deepest position briefly. Feel the stretch in your left adductor and the load in your right leg.
Drive through your right foot to stand back up.
Shift to the left side and repeat.
Continue alternating for the desired total reps.
Builds hip mobility and adductor flexibility
Develops unilateral leg strength
Trains balance and coordination
Excellent warm-up for lower-body training
No equipment needed
Improves squat depth over time

description.en: The cross arms push-up performs a push-up with the hands crossed under the chest, one stacked over the other. The crossed hand position challenges balance, core stability, and shoulder stabilizers. It is a unique advanced bodyweight push-up variation.

en: Get into a push-up position with hands under your chest.
Cross one hand over the other so they are stacked.
Set your feet wider than usual for balance.
Brace your core hard and keep your body in a straight line.
Bend your elbows to lower your chest toward your hands.
Stop when your chest is just above the hands.
Press through your hands to drive back up.
Maintain control throughout the entire rep.
Challenges balance
Builds core stability
Strengthens shoulder stabilizers
No equipment required
Advanced push-up variation
Useful for stability work

description.en: The decline knee raise lies on a decline bench with head at the high end and raises the knees toward the chest. The decline angle increases gravity resistance compared to flat knee raises, providing greater lower ab loading.

en: Lie on a decline bench with your head at the high end. Grip the bench or handles behind your head.
Legs extended down the decline.
Raise both knees toward your chest by curling your hips up.
Continue until your knees are near your chest and your hips lift off the bench.
Squeeze your lower abs at the top.
Lower under control back to the extended position.
Do not swing or use momentum.
Aim for 12 to 15 reps per set.
Greater lower ab loading from decline angle
Builds lower ab strength beyond flat knee raises
Hip curl component targets the lower abs
Simple setup
Progressive — adjust decline angle for difficulty
Useful for ab hypertrophy

description.en: The dumbbell glute bridge is a hip extension exercise performed lying on the floor with a dumbbell held across the hips. It directly targets the glutes with no bench or rack required, making it one of the most accessible glute-building exercises for home training. It is an excellent regression from the hip thrust or an effective standalone exercise.

en: Lie flat on your back with knees bent at roughly 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Place a dumbbell across your hips, just below your hip bones. Hold it in place with both hands.
Brace your core, tuck your chin slightly, and press your lower back gently into the floor.
Drive through your heels and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips off the floor.
Continue until your body forms a straight line from your knees to your shoulders. Your shins should be roughly vertical at the top.
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top for one to two seconds. Do not hyperextend your lower back.
Lower your hips under control back to the floor.
Briefly touch the floor, then drive up again. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Direct glute isolation with no bench required
Easy to do at home with one dumbbell
Easier on the lower back than many other glute exercises
Good regression from the hip thrust
Builds glute activation and strength
Easy to scale by using a heavier dumbbell

description.en: The dumbbell goblet curtsey lunge combines the curtsey lunge pattern with a goblet hold. Holding the dumbbell at your chest, you step one leg diagonally behind the other into a curtsey position. The crossover pattern hits the gluteus medius and adductors more than a standard lunge.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell vertically at your chest with both hands.
Brace your core and stand tall.
Step your right leg diagonally behind and across your left leg into a curtsey position.
Bend both knees to lower into the curtsey lunge.
Keep your torso upright and front foot flat.
Continue down until your back knee approaches the floor behind your front leg.
Drive through the front foot to step back to the starting position.
Repeat on the other side, alternating curtseys.
Hits gluteus medius and adductors
Builds hip stability
Trains diagonal movement patterns
Strong glute development
Improves balance and coordination
Useful for athletes who need lateral stability

description.en: The dumbbell incline hammer press performs an incline dumbbell press with a neutral (hammer/palms-facing) grip. The neutral grip is more shoulder-friendly than pronated pressing and the incline angle targets the upper chest. It is ideal for lifters with shoulder issues.

en: Set an incline bench to 30 to 45 degrees. Lie back with dumbbells at your chest, palms facing each other (neutral grip).
Press both dumbbells straight up while maintaining the neutral grip.
Lock out at the top. The dumbbells may touch at the top.
Lower under control back to your chest.
Maintain neutral grip throughout — palms always face each other.
The neutral grip is easier on the shoulders than pronated grip.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Excellent for lifters with shoulder impingement.
Shoulder-friendly neutral grip
Incline angle targets upper chest
Ideal for lifters with shoulder issues
Easy to load progressively
Effective for upper chest hypertrophy
Reduces front delt dominance

description.en: The dumbbell incline head supported row is performed face down on an incline bench with the forehead and chest supported. The full body support eliminates lower back stress and body english entirely, allowing strict back rowing form. It is one of the strictest possible row variations.

en: Set an incline bench to about 45 degrees.
Lie face down on the bench with your chest and forehead supported.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand with arms hanging down.
Use a neutral grip with palms facing each other.
Brace your core.
Row the dumbbells up by driving your elbows back toward your hips.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower the dumbbells back down with control to a full stretch.
Ultra-strict rowing form
Eliminates all body english
Chest and head support reduces strain
Builds back size and thickness
Strong lat and rhomboid engagement
Useful for hypertrophy training

description.en: The dumbbell incline one arm lateral raise is performed lying on the side on an incline bench, holding a dumbbell with the top arm. The position eliminates body english and the bench support extends the bottom range, increasing time under tension on the side delt. It is a strong choice for side delt isolation.

en: Set a bench to a 30 to 45 degree incline.
Lie on your side on the bench with your bottom arm bent under your head.
Hold a dumbbell in your top hand with palm facing down toward your hip.
Brace your core and pull your shoulder back.
Maintain a slight bend in the elbow.
Raise the dumbbell out to the side in a controlled arc.
Continue until your arm is roughly perpendicular to the floor.
Squeeze the side delt at the top, then lower with control to the starting position. Switch sides.
Strict single-arm side delt isolation
Bench support extends bottom range
Eliminates body english
Builds side delt size and detail
Strong mind-muscle connection
Useful for shoulder specialization

description.en: The dumbbell incline tricep extension performs lying tricep extensions on an incline bench. The incline angle increases the stretch on the long head of the tricep at the bottom, providing a greater stimulus than flat bench extensions.

en: Set an incline bench to 30 to 45 degrees. Sit and lean back with a dumbbell in each hand.
Press the dumbbells above your chest, arms extended.
Keep upper arms vertical. Bend at the elbows to lower the dumbbells behind your head.
Lower until you feel a deep stretch in your triceps.
Extend your elbows to press back to lockout.
Squeeze your triceps at the top.
The incline increases the long-head stretch.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Increased long-head stretch from incline angle
Greater stimulus than flat bench extensions
Builds tricep size through full range
Easy to set up
Each arm works independently
Useful for tricep development

description.en: The dumbbell seated tricep extension is an overhead tricep extension performed seated with a single heavy dumbbell held with both hands. The seated position with back support eliminates body english, and the overhead position stretches the tricep long head for maximum activation.

en: Sit on a bench with back support. Hold a single dumbbell with both hands, gripping the top end.
Press the dumbbell overhead with arms extended.
Keep upper arms vertical, pointing toward the ceiling.
Bend at the elbows to lower the dumbbell behind your head.
Lower until you feel a deep tricep stretch.
Extend back to lockout by straightening your elbows.
Squeeze your triceps at the top.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
Targets the tricep long head with overhead stretch
Seated position eliminates momentum
Back support ensures clean form
Only one dumbbell needed
Easy to load progressively
Builds tricep size

description.en: The dumbbell standing one arm concentration curl performs the concentration curl from a standing position, hinged forward at the hips. Bracing the working elbow against the inner thigh allows strict bicep isolation without sitting. The standing position adds a small core engagement and is useful when no bench is available.

en: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width apart, soft bend in the knees.
Hold a single dumbbell in your right hand.
Hinge forward at the hips and rest your right elbow against your inner right thigh.
Allow the dumbbell to hang at full arm extension.
Place your left hand on your left thigh for support.
Curl the dumbbell up by bending only at the elbow.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower the dumbbell back down with control. Switch arms.
Strict bicep peak isolation
Builds bicep size
No bench required
Strong stretch at the bottom
Eliminates body english
Useful for home or travel training

description.en: The exercise ball back extension with arms extended is a back extension done over a stability ball with the arms held straight overhead. The extended arm position lengthens the lever and increases load on the lower back.

en: Lie face down with the hips supported on a stability ball.
Set the feet wide on the floor for stability.
Reach the arms straight out overhead.
Brace the core and keep the body relaxed at the start.
Lift the chest off the ball by extending the back.
Continue lifting until the body forms a straight line.
Squeeze the lower back and glutes at the top.
Lower with control to the start.
Builds the lower back.
Trains the glutes.
Extended arms add lever load.
Joint friendly back work.
Useful for posture.

description.en: The exercise ball serratus wall slide is a scapular activation drill. Rolling a stability ball up a wall with the forearms while reaching overhead trains the serratus anterior to upwardly rotate the shoulder blades.

en: Stand facing a wall with a stability ball at chest height.
Place both forearms on the ball with the elbows bent.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Roll the ball up the wall by reaching the arms overhead.
Press the arms forward to upwardly rotate the shoulder blades.
Reach up as far as possible with the elbows close.
Roll the ball back down with control.
Continue for the working set.
Activates the serratus anterior.
Improves overhead mobility.
Builds shoulder health.
Useful warm-up.
Trains scapular control.

description.en: The ez bar incline front raise is performed lying face-up on an incline bench. An EZ bar is held below shoulder level and raised straight up in front. The bench support eliminates body swing and the angled grip on the EZ bar reduces wrist strain. It builds the front delts with strict form.

en: Set an incline bench to about 45 degrees.
Lie face up on the bench with feet flat on the floor.
Hold an EZ curl bar at the angled grips with palms down.
Brace your core and keep your back against the bench.
Start with the bar resting on your thighs.
Raise the bar straight up and forward in front of you.
Lift until the bar is at about shoulder height.
Lower the bar slowly back to the start.
Strict front delt isolation
No body swing
Reduces wrist strain
Builds the front deltoids
Bench-supported strict form
Strong shoulder isolation

description.en: The ez barbell close grip curl is a curl variation using a narrow grip on the ez bar. The lifter grips the inner curves of the bar with the hands close together, then curls. The narrow grip biases the long head of the biceps and trains the outer biceps.

en: Stand tall holding an ez curl bar with hands on the inner curves close together.
Set the elbows tight against the sides.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Curl the bar up toward the chest by bending the elbows.
Keep the elbows fixed at the sides throughout.
Continue curling until the bar reaches the upper chest.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower the bar back down with control.
Strong long head bicep builder
Builds the outer biceps
Trains the brachialis
Builds bicep size
Useful arm builder
Strong ez bar move

description.en: The EZ-bar drag bicep curl is a variation of the drag curl using the angled grip of an EZ bar. The bar drags up the front of the body while the elbows pull back behind the torso. This removes most front delt involvement and places nearly all the work on the biceps. The EZ bar is also wrist-friendly compared to a straight bar.

en: Stand tall holding an EZ bar with a shoulder-width underhand grip.
Let the bar hang at your thighs.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Curl the bar by pulling your elbows backward, dragging the bar up your torso.
Keep the bar in contact with or close to your body the entire time.
Lift until the bar reaches your lower chest.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower the bar slowly to the start.
Maximum biceps isolation
Wrist-friendly EZ bar grip
Removes front delt involvement
Builds biceps peak and thickness
Strong mind-muscle connection
Useful for biceps hypertrophy

description.en: Finger curls are a deep grip exercise where you start with a barbell in your palms and let it roll down to your fingertips, then curl it back up using only your finger flexors. It builds the forearm flexors and crushing grip strength. It is one of the best exercises for grip development.

en: Sit on a bench. Place your forearms on the bench with wrists hanging off the edge, palms up.
Hold a barbell with an underhand grip.
Open your fingers and let the bar roll down to your fingertips.
Once at your fingertips, curl your fingers back to bring the bar back into your palms.
Then curl your wrist up for additional flexion.
Slowly reverse — extend your wrist, then let the bar roll back to your fingertips.
The finger roll is the key — most of the work is the finger flexors.
Use light weight. Aim for 15 to 20 reps.
Builds the forearm flexors (extreme)
Develops crushing grip strength
Targets finger flexors directly
Useful for climbing, grappling, and lifting
Easy to load progressively
Excellent grip exercise

description.en: The incline scapula push-up is performed in an incline push-up position with hands on a bench or against a wall. With straight arms, the shoulder blades retract and protract through full scapular range. It strengthens the serratus anterior and is great for shoulder health and posture.

en: Place your hands on a sturdy bench or against a wall.
Walk your feet back to a high incline push-up position.
Keep your arms straight throughout the entire movement.
Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line.
Allow your shoulder blades to squeeze together (retract).
Your chest will dip slightly toward your hands.
Push through your hands to spread the shoulder blades apart (protract).
Round your upper back at the top of each rep.
Strengthens the serratus anterior
Improves scapular control
Beginner-friendly variation
Useful for shoulder health
Builds pressing stability
No equipment beyond a bench

description.en: The kettlebell bent over alternate twist row is a single-arm row variation that adds a torso twist on each rep. The lifter rows one kettlebell at a time from a bent over position while rotating the torso slightly toward the working side. The twist loads the obliques.

en: Stand holding a kettlebell in each hand at the sides.
Hinge at the hips with a flat back and slight knee bend.
Let the kettlebells hang down with palms facing each other.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Row one kettlebell up to the hip while rotating the torso slightly.
Squeeze the lat hard at the top.
Lower with control while rotating the torso back to neutral.
Row the other kettlebell while rotating to that side. Alternate sides.
Combo back and core move
Trains rotational strength
Builds lat thickness
Strong unilateral row
Useful back-day move
Builds rotational core

description.en: The kettlebell rear lunge is essentially the same as the kettlebell backward lunge — stepping backward into a lunge while holding kettlebells. This page uses the "rear lunge" naming convention. It is knee-friendly and maintains tension on the front leg.

en: Stand tall holding KBs at your sides or in the front rack.
Step your right foot back two to three feet.
Lower your right knee toward the floor.
Drive through your left (front) foot to return to standing.
Alternate legs or complete all reps on one side.
Keep torso upright throughout.
Use moderate weight.
Aim for 8 to 12 reps per leg.
Knee-friendly lunge variation
Builds quad and glute strength unilaterally
Easy to scale with KB weight
Maintains tension on the front leg
Exposes imbalances
Simple setup

description.en: The kneeling neck stretch is a gentle seated neck stretch performed in a kneeling or seated position. The stable base lets you focus fully on lengthening the neck and upper traps without compensation. It is a great option for relieving desk-related neck pain and tension.

en: Kneel on the floor and sit your hips back onto your heels.
Place your hands on your thighs.
Sit up tall through the spine.
Slowly tilt your head to one side, bringing the ear toward the shoulder.
Avoid forcing the stretch or shrugging the shoulder.
Hold for a comfortable duration.
Return to center and tilt to the other side.
Continue alternating sides.
Relieves neck tension
Stretches the upper traps
Useful for desk workers
Stable kneeling base
Easy and gentle on the body

description.en: The lever donkey calf raise is a calf exercise performed on a dedicated donkey calf raise machine. Bent forward at the hips with a padded lever across your lower back, you raise and lower your heels against the machine resistance. The hip-flexed position puts the gastrocnemius under a deeper stretch than standing raises, driving more growth stimulus.

en: Step onto the donkey calf raise machine. Place the balls of your feet on the edge of the foot platform with heels hanging off.
Position the padded lever across your lower back (hips, not spine). Grip the handles.
Your torso should be bent forward at roughly 90 degrees with your back flat.
Let your heels drop as low as possible into a deep calf stretch.
Push through the balls of your feet to rise up onto your toes as high as possible.
Squeeze your calves hard at the top for one to two seconds.
Lower under control back to the deep stretch over two to three seconds.
Repeat for 12 to 20+ reps per set.
Hip-flexed position stretches the gastrocnemius more than standing raises
Adjustable machine loading for progressive overload
Deep stretch at the bottom drives growth
Guided motion provides consistent form
Excellent calf mass builder
Easier to set up than partner donkey calf raises

description.en: The push up inside leg kick is a push up variation that adds a leg kick at the top. The lifter performs a push up, then at the top lifts one leg up and kicks it across the body under the other arm. The kick adds rotation and core challenge.

en: Begin in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders.
Set the body in a straight line from head to heels.
Brace your core hard.
Lower the chest toward the floor by bending the elbows.
Press back up to lockout.
At the top lift one leg up and kick it through across the body.
Bring the leg back to the start.
Repeat the push up and kick the other leg on the next rep.
Combo chest and core builder
Trains rotational core
Builds the glutes
Strong push up variation
Useful core builder
Strong functional pattern

description.en: The resistance band standing external rotation is a rotator cuff drill done standing with a band anchored at elbow height. The lifter pins the elbow to the side and rotates the forearm outward. It is a useful shoulder health move.

en: Anchor a resistance band at elbow height.
Stand sideways to the anchor.
Grip the band handle with the working arm.
Pin the elbow to the side at ninety degrees.
Bring the forearm across the body to the start.
Brace your core and keep the elbow tucked.
Rotate the forearm outward away from the body.
Return with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Builds the rotator cuff
Strong shoulder health drill
Trains external rotation
Useful warm-up
Builds shoulder stability

description.en: The resistance band standing single arm lateral shoulder extension is a unilateral rear delt drill. Pressing one arm out to the side and slightly back against band tension isolates the rear delt and exposes side to side weakness.

en: Anchor a resistance band at chest height in front of you.
Stand facing the anchor.
Grab the band with one hand at chest level.
Step back to set tension and stand tall.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Pull the arm out to the side and slightly back.
Squeeze the rear delt at the end range.
Return with control and continue for all reps then switch.
Isolates the rear delt.
Trains one side at a time.
Band tension grows through the range.
Useful for posture.
Builds the upper back.

description.en: The lever reverse vertical hack squat is performed facing the machine pad rather than facing away. The reverse position shifts more emphasis to the glutes and hamstrings while still loading the quads. It is a strong glute-focused hack squat variation popular in modern bodybuilding gyms.

en: Step into the hack squat machine and face the back pad.
Place your shoulders against the shoulder pads.
Position your feet shoulder-width apart on the platform.
Release the safety handles and brace your core.
Lower yourself by bending the knees and sitting your hips back.
Continue down until your thighs are parallel to the platform.
Drive through your heels to stand back up.
Squeeze the glutes hard at the top.
Glute-focused hack squat variation
Stable, guided path
Hits the quads and glutes together
Reduces lower back strain
Easy to scale heavy
Useful for leg day

description.en: The roll back stretch is a Pilates-style mobility exercise where you sit with knees bent, hold your shins, and rock back and forth on your rounded spine like a rocking chair. It massages the back muscles, decompresses the spine, and teaches segmental spinal articulation.

en: Sit on the floor with knees bent and feet flat. Hug your knees with both arms.
Tuck your chin to your chest. Round your back fully — like a ball.
Lift your feet off the floor. Balance on your sit bones.
Roll backward by tipping your hips back, allowing your spine to roll along the floor sequentially.
Roll only as far as your shoulder blades — do not roll onto your neck.
Reverse the roll, using core control to come back up to seated.
Maintain the rounded back and tucked chin throughout.
Repeat 6 to 10 times. Use a mat for cushioning.
Massages the back muscles
Decompresses the spine
Teaches segmental spinal articulation
Improves core control
No equipment needed (mat recommended)
Pilates foundational exercise

description.en: The safety bar good morning is a hip-hinge exercise performed with a safety squat bar (yoke bar with handles) instead of a standard barbell. The bar's shape allows you to grip handles in front rather than holding the bar across your back, dramatically reducing shoulder demand. It is the most comfortable good morning variation for lifters with shoulder mobility issues.

en: Set up a safety squat bar in a power rack at upper-chest height.
Step under the bar and let the pads rest across your upper back. Grip the front handles.
Unrack the bar and step back. Stand with feet hip-width apart.
Brace your core. Set a soft, fixed bend in your knees.
Hinge forward at the hips by pushing your butt back. Keep your back flat.
Lower until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor or until you feel a strong hamstring stretch.
Drive your hips forward to stand back up. Squeeze your glutes at the top.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Most comfortable good morning variation for tight shoulders
Eliminates the need to hold a barbell across the back
Builds the posterior chain — hamstrings, glutes, and lower back
Allows heavier loading for many lifters
Useful for lifters with shoulder mobility issues
Excellent posterior chain accessory exercise

description.en: The seated side to side leg raise crunch on the floor sits in a V position with the legs lifted. Sweeping the knees from side to side hammers the obliques and lower abs together.

en: Sit on the floor with the knees bent and feet off the ground.
Lean back slightly to engage the core.
Place the hands on the floor behind for support.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Sweep the bent knees to one side with control.
Use the obliques to bring them back through center.
Sweep the knees to the other side.
Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions.
Hammers the obliques and lower abs.
Builds rotational core strength.
No equipment needed.
Carryover to athletic rotation.
Easy to scale by adjusting leg height.
Develops total core endurance.

description.en: The shoulder tap push-up adds a shoulder tap between each push-up — at the top of each rep, you alternately touch your opposite shoulder with your hand while balancing on the other arm. The added single-arm balance demand dramatically increases core and shoulder engagement.

en: Get into a high plank position with hands shoulder-width apart, body in a straight line.
Brace your core hard. Keep your hips stable.
Lower your chest to the floor in a push-up.
Press back up to the top of the push-up.
At the top, lift your right hand off the floor and tap your left shoulder.
Return your right hand to the floor.
Lower into another push-up. At the top, tap your right shoulder with your left hand.
Continue alternating taps after each push-up. Keep hips perfectly still during the taps.
Adds significant core engagement to push-ups
Trains anti-rotation strength
Builds shoulder stability
No equipment needed
Easy to scale by adjusting tempo or removing taps
Engaging push-up variation

description.en: The silent burpee is a low-impact variation of the standard burpee. Without the jump at the top or the harsh landing in the plank, the movement stays quiet and joint-friendly. The slower controlled pattern still builds full body conditioning while being apartment-friendly and easier on the joints.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Squat down and place your hands on the floor in front of your feet.
Step one foot back, then the other into a high plank position.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
Lower your chest to the floor in a push up.
Press back up to the plank position.
Step one foot forward, then the other back to the squat position.
Stand up tall without jumping at the top.
Low-impact full body conditioning
Apartment-friendly and quiet
Joint-friendly variation
Builds endurance
No jumping or harsh landing
Useful for cardio circuits

description.en: The skater squat is a single-leg squat where the non-working leg bends behind you (like a skating lunge) rather than extending forward like a pistol squat. You squat down on one leg while the other knee hovers behind. It requires less hip flexor flexibility than pistol squats.

en: Stand on your right leg. Bend your left knee behind you so your left foot hovers behind.
Extend your arms forward for counterbalance.
Squat down on your right leg — sitting back and down.
Lower until your left knee lightly touches the floor (or a pad).
Drive through your right foot to stand back up.
Complete reps, then switch legs.
Place a pad behind you for the rear knee to touch for depth reference.
Aim for 5 to 10 reps per leg.
Single-leg squat without hip flexor flexibility demands
Builds quad and glute strength unilaterally
Requires less flexibility than pistol squats
No equipment needed
Develops balance and control
Useful for athletes

description.en: The squat thrust is a full-body conditioning exercise similar to a burpee but without the jump. You squat down, kick your feet back to a plank, jump your feet back to a squat, and stand. It builds cardiovascular conditioning and full-body endurance.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
Squat down and place your hands on the floor in front of you.
Kick both feet back to land in a plank position.
Immediately jump your feet back to the squat position.
Stand up.
That is one rep. Continue at a brisk pace.
No push-up or jump needed — just the squat-plank-squat-stand cycle.
Aim for 10 to 20 reps per set or work for time.
Full-body conditioning without impact from jumping
Builds cardiovascular endurance
Easier than burpees
No equipment needed
Develops speed and agility
Useful for circuit training

description.en: The standing reach up back rotation stretch is a thoracic mobility drill. Reaching one arm overhead and rotating the trunk to the same side stretches the obliques and lats while opening the upper back.

en: Stand tall with the feet shoulder width apart.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Reach one arm straight up overhead.
Rotate the torso slowly toward the working side.
Continue rotating until the chest faces back.
Hold the rotated position briefly.
Return to center and switch sides.
Continue alternating for the working set.
Mobilizes the thoracic spine.
Stretches the obliques.
Opens the lats.
Useful warm-up.
Improves rotational mobility.

description.en: The strongman deadlift refers to deadlift variations specific to strongman competitions, typically performed with a thicker bar (axle bar), elevated handles, or specialty implements like Atlas stones. They build elite full-body pulling strength using awkward, heavy implements. Standard barbell technique applies but with greater grip and core demand.

en: Set up the implement (axle bar, deadlift bar, or trap bar) loaded with significant weight.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, the bar over the middle of your feet.
Hinge at the hips and bend your knees to grip the bar with both hands.
Brace your core hard. Lift your chest. Pull the slack out of the bar.
Drive through your full feet, pushing the floor away. Pull the bar up your shins as your hips rise.
Stand tall at the top with shoulders back, hips fully locked out.
Lower the bar under control by hinging at the hips first, then bending the knees.
Use straps if grip fails before the legs and back. Strongman implements are unforgiving.
Builds elite full-body pulling strength
Develops grip strength with thicker bars
Trains odd-object handling
Strongman competition staple
Carries over to all heavy lifting
Builds mental toughness

description.en: Mas wrestling is a traditional strength sport where two opponents sit facing each other with feet braced against a board, gripping a stick between them. On the signal, each pulls the stick toward themselves. The winner either takes the stick or pulls the opponent over the board. It tests full-body pulling strength.

en: Two opponents sit facing each other on the floor with feet braced against a dividing board.
Both grip a sturdy stick (mas wrestling stick) between them.
On the signal, each athlete pulls the stick toward themselves.
Win by pulling the stick from the opponent or pulling them over the board.
Use full-body pulling — legs drive against the board, back and arms pull.
Maintain grip at all costs.
This is a traditional sport from Yakutia (Sakha Republic, Russia).
Practice with a training partner and proper equipment.
Tests full-body pulling strength
Traditional strength sport
Builds grip, back, and leg drive
Competitive and engaging
Develops pulling power
Builds mental toughness

description.en: The superman row with towel combines a superman back extension with a towel row pattern. The lifter lies face down in a superman pose with a towel held overhead and pulls the towel ends apart while squeezing the upper back. The combo trains the entire back chain.

en: Lie face down on a mat with the legs straight.
Hold a towel taut between your hands extended overhead.
Lift the chest, arms, and legs off the floor into a superman.
Brace your core and squeeze the glutes.
Pull the towel apart while pulling the elbows back.
Squeeze the upper back hard at the top.
Hold the squeeze briefly.
Release the pull and lower back down with control.
Combo back move
Trains lower and upper back
No major equipment needed
Strong posture builder
Builds back endurance
Useful warm-up move

description.en: The supported squat holds onto a stable object (pole, door frame, TRX strap, or squat rack) for balance assistance while performing bodyweight squats. It is the most beginner-friendly squat regression, allowing people with balance or mobility limitations to practice the squat pattern safely.

en: Stand in front of a sturdy pole, door frame, or rack upright. Grip it with both hands at chest height.
Set feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out.
Sit your hips back and down into a squat while lightly holding the support.
Use the support for balance — not to pull yourself up. Your legs do the work.
Descend as deep as your mobility allows.
Drive through your feet to stand.
Progressively use less hand support as your balance improves.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps per set.
Most beginner-friendly squat regression
Allows practice for people with balance limitations
Builds squat pattern confidence
Easy to scale by reducing hand support over time
Safe and accessible
Progresses naturally toward unassisted squats

description.en: The suspender rear delt row uses a TRX or suspension trainer for a horizontal row with the elbows flared out high. The high-elbow path shifts emphasis from the lats to the rear delts and upper back. It is a great rear delt builder that requires only a suspension trainer.

en: Set a suspension trainer at about chest height.
Grab both handles with palms facing down.
Lean back with arms extended and feet planted.
Brace your core and keep your body straight.
Row by pulling your elbows out to the sides at shoulder height.
Lead with the elbows and squeeze the shoulder blades together.
Keep your hands wider than your elbows at the top.
Lower with control and repeat.
Targets the rear delts
Builds upper back strength
Adjustable difficulty via foot position
Improves posture
Useful for shoulder health
No weights required

description.en: The twist Superman adds a rotational twist to the standard Superman exercise. From a lying face-down position, you lift the chest and legs into a Superman, then twist the torso to one side at the top. The rotation adds oblique and erector spinae work to the standard back extension.

en: Lie face down on the floor with arms extended overhead.
Position your legs straight with toes pointed.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
Lift your chest, arms, and legs off the floor in a Superman position.
Hold the lifted position briefly.
Twist your torso to the right while staying lifted.
Return to center, then twist to the left.
Lower back to the floor with control.
Builds back extension strength
Adds rotational core work
Strong oblique engagement
Strong glute activation
No equipment required
Useful for posterior chain training

description.en: The weighted plate overhead march holds a weight plate overhead while marching in place. The overhead position loads the shoulders and the marching motion challenges core stability. It is a strong combo move for shoulders and core.

en: Hold a weight plate with both hands overhead.
Stand with the feet hip width apart.
Lock out the elbows overhead.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
March in place by lifting one knee up high.
Lower the leg and lift the other knee up.
Keep the plate stable overhead throughout.
Continue marching in place.
Builds the shoulders
Trains the core
Strong combo move
Useful for athletes
Builds overhead stability

description.en: The weighted stretch lunge holds a deep lunge position with light dumbbells overhead or at the sides for added load during the stretch. The loading deepens the hip flexor stretch on the back leg while training stability through the front leg. It is a strong choice for hip mobility work.

en: Hold a light dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Step forward into a deep lunge with your right leg.
Lower your back knee toward the floor.
Keep your front shin vertical with the knee over the ankle.
Press your back hip forward and down for a hip flexor stretch.
Brace your core and stand tall through the torso.
Hold the deep lunge position for the duration of the stretch.
Release the lunge and switch sides.
Loads the hip flexor stretch for deeper opening
Builds stability through the front leg
Improves hip mobility
Trains lunge endurance
Strong glute activation on the back leg
Useful for hip mobility programs
